PAPER: Artificial Intelligence Review (2026) 59:31 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11442-0 Graph network learning for human skeleton modeling: a survey Xi Yang1 · Shaoyi Li1 · Saisai Niu2 · Xiaokui Yue1 Received: 6 April 2025 / Accepted: 30 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Over the past few decades, Human Skeleton Modeling (HSM) has gained considerable attention in computer vision, exploring various practical applications such as the video surveillance, the human-computer interaction, the medical assistance analysis, and the autonomous driving through images and videos. The performance of HSM and its applica- tions on challenging datasets has been significantly improved due to recent advancements of deep learning methods. These advancements have been extended to non-Euclidean or graph data with multiple nodes and edges. Because human joints and skeleton combina- tions are represented as graph structures, graph networks are appropriate for the non- Euclidean HSM. In recent years, graph networks have become essential tools for the HSM and behavioral analyses. However, prior surveys are often siloed, focusing either on a narrow class of models such as GCNs or on a single application like action recognition. A unified framework that systematically analyzes diverse graph network learning paradigms across the entire HSM pipeline has been notably absent. We conduct a survey of graph network methods for HSM and their application domains. This comprehensive overview includes a taxonomy of graph network techniques, a detailed study of benchmark datasets for HSM, extensive descriptions of the performance of graph networks in three major ap- plication domains, and a collection of related resources and open-source codes. Finally, we provided insightful recommendations for future research directions and trends of graph networks for HSM. This survey serves as the introductory material for beginners in graph network-based HSM and as the reference materials for advanced researchers. HSM can be utilized to locate and identify the key joints of the human skeleton, connect them to form a projection on the two-dimensional plane of an image, and obtain the human skeleton structure. The primary task of the 3D HSM involves predicting the three- dimensional coordinates and angles of the human skeletal joints. Owing to the scarcity of annotated human skeleton datasets, most research methods have been based on existing HSM approaches. Methods for HSM can be categorized into two main classes: traditional (Meyer et al. 2011) and deep learning-based methods (Lan et al. 2023). Before the widespread adoption of deep learning, datasets for the skeletal motion and high-performance computing plat- forms were not ubiquitous. Consequently, researchers have primarily employed the tradi- tional computer vision and machine learning techniques for skeleton modeling. Although the traditional methods exhibit the high temporal efficiency, they primarily rely on manually engineered features, such as the histogram of oriented gradient (HOG) (Dalal and Triggs 2005) and scale invariant feature transform (SIFT) (Al Ghamdi et al. 2012). In the context of HSM, the human skeleton is naturally represented as a graph, where joints correspond to nodes and physical or functional connections between joints are represented as edges. This representation allows Graph Networks to capture the intricate spatial and temporal dependencies inherent in skeletal motion data. At the core of graph networks is the message passing paradigm, which enables each node (i.e., a joint) to iteratively update its feature representation by aggregating information from its neighbors. This process precisely mimics the inter-dependencies among joints in human motion–for instance, the state of the wrist is clearly influenced by the states of the elbow and hand. This process can be described by a general graph convolution equation: h′i =σ( A ij Wh j +b), (1) j ∈∑N (i) where, h j is the feature vector of a neighboring joint v j. In HSM, this can be a multi-dimen- sional vector containing its 3D coordinates, velocity, or orientation, describing the joint’s current kinematic state. (i) represents the set of neighboring nodes for joint v i, typically N defined by the inherent physical connections of the human body. A ij is an element from the adjacency matrix, defining the "weight" or "strength" of the information passed from joint v j to v i. This can be a simple binary value (indicating physical connection) or a learnable parameter that expresses the importance of different connections (e.g., the shoulder-elbow connection is more structurally significant than a non-physical wrist-head connection). W is a learnable weight matrix that acts as a "feature transformer," applying a linear transforma- tion to the neighbor’s features h j before they are aggregated. Functionally, it learns how to extract the most relevant patterns from the raw states of the neighbors for the target task. This simulates the process where the target joint considers the states of all ∑ its relevant body parts. b is a bias term, and σ is a non-linear activation function. As human motion is a highly complex, non-linear process, the activation function is crucial for captur- ing this complexity. h ′i is the updated feature vector for joint v i. After one round of message passing, it now incorporates contextual information from its local neighborhood, leading to a more robust and richer representation of its own state. While graph networks provide a powerful theoretical framework for HSM, their basic forms also reveal inherent limitations when facing real-world complexities. The effective- ness of these models relies heavily on the completeness and accuracy of the input skeleton graph data. In practical scenarios, challenges such as occlusion are extremely common. When body joints are occluded, their corresponding node features can be missing or noisy, which severely disrupts the message-passing mechanism that graph networks depend on and degrades the accuracy of the overall pose. Similarly, significant viewpoint variations pose another challenge. A Graph network trained on a specific view may struggle to gener- alize to a drastically different one because the projected spatial relationships and distances between joints change fundamentally, potentially confusing a model with fixed relational assumptions. Furthermore, a basic graph network typically employs a predefined and static graph topology, which constrains its expressive power. For actions like hugging or shaking hands, a strong, temporary functional relationship is established between the hands, yet no such edge exists in the standard skeleton topology. These limitations highlight the need for more advanced and adaptive graph network architectures to improve robustness and expres- siveness in complex, real-world environments. Previous approaches to categorizing the literature have often implicitly relied on two main schemes: one is application-based, dividing methods into categories like action recognition or pose estimation; the other is model-family-based, grouping together variants of a specific architecture such as ST-GCN. However, these approaches have limitations. An application-based grouping obscures underlying methodological differences, while a model-family-based grouping can devolve into a "laundry list" of methods that lacks high-level insight. The "locus of innovation" taxonomy proposed in this study offers a more fundamental and insightful perspective. Its superiority is threefold: first, it moves beyond a surface-level focus on a model’s application to an essential analysis of its core innovative mechanism, distinguishing between innovations in graph structure versus those in operational modules. Second, this systematic framework helps reveal deeper developmental trajectories in the field, showing an evolution from an initial focus on module-based innovations on fixed graphs toward more recent and fundamental work on the graph structure itself. Therefore, this taxonomy serves not merely as an organizational tool, but as an analytical one, enabling readers to better understand the logical evolution of the field and its future directions. 1 3 31 Page 12 of 57 X. As shown in Fig. 5, these models utilize the natural topological graph structure of human skeletons to capture the spatial and temporal dependencies, enhancing their mod- eling capability for human poses and actions. Spatio-temporal graph networks aggregate skeletal joints across different time steps by performing CNN operations in the temporal dimension, utilizing the temporal relationships for the feature extraction and learning. This approach can effectively encode the dynamic variations in human skeletons and capture the joint positions and the motion patterns across different frames. One prominent model in this field is the spatio-temporal GCN (ST-GCN) (Yan et al. 2018). The authors first applied the GCN in the action recognition and proposed an ST-GCN for the general modeling of dynamic skeletons. The ST-GCN treated human skeletal joints as the nodes, spatially connected the joints in the human skeleton as the spatial edges, and temporally aggregated the corresponding nodes across previo us and subsequent frames as the temporal edges. A spatio-temporal graph is represented as, G= { G 1 ,G 2 , ··· ,G N } , where G 1 ,G 2 , ··· ,G N represent the input skeleton graph in each frame, and N denotes the total number of frames. Subsequently, multiple layers of the spatio-temporal GCN are constructed on this spatio-temporal graph to extract information separately in the spatial and temporal dimensions. This model has been widely applied to action recognition tasks to achieve the state-of-the-art performance on large datasets. Furthermore, several improve- ments to ST-GCN have been proposed to enhance the recognition accuracy, including MST- GCN (Chen et al. 2021), MST-GNN (Li et al. 2021), ST-BLN (Heidari and Iosifidis 2021), WST-GCN (Miki et al. 2020), Stacked-STGCN (Ghosh et al. 2020), DSTD-GC (Fu et al. 2022), ST-PGN (Parsa et al. 2020). These datasets share the common characteristic of con- taining human motion data in real-world settings, covering a range of categories, such as daily activities, with both authenticity and diversity. These are often collected using multi- view setups and provide 2D or 3D human joint information, which is beneficial for motion predictions. Some datasets utilize the motion capture technology for high-precision data, whereas others use data from Internet videos. The large number of samples in these datasets meet the demands of model research. Several metrics were used to evaluate the performance of the HSM models. For pose estimation, the mean per joint position error (MPJPE) (Wang et al. 2021a) calculates the Euclidean distance between the estimated 3D joints and the ground truth positions, reflecting the accuracy of the 3D pose estimation. The percentage of correct parts (PCP) (Wang et al. 2021a) is determined when the distance between the predicted and ground truth joints was less than a fraction of the limb length, typically between 0.1 and 0.5. The percentage of correct keypoints (PCK) (Wang et al. 2021a) measures the accuracy of keypoint localization within a certain threshold, which is set to 50% of the head segment length of each test image. The intersection over union (IoU) (Wang et al. 2021b) identi- fies differences between the ground-truth annotations and predicted bounding boxes, with unnecessary predicted boxes removed based on a designated threshold (typically 0.5). The object keypoint similarity (OKS) (Wang et al. 2021b) is the average similarity of all object keypoints, calculated based on the subject’s scale and the distance between the predicted points and ground truth points using scale and keypoint constants to equalize the weight of each keypoint. The average precision (AP) measures the accuracy of keypoint detection based on Precision, representing the average precision of all recall values between 0 and 1 across various IoU thresholds. The average recall (AR) evaluates the accuracy of keypoint detection based on the recall, representing the average recall of all recall values between 0 and 1 across various IoU thresholds. Several evaluation metrics are commonly used for human-action recognition. Accuracy is the most common metric and is calculated as the proportion of correctly classified sam- ples. F1 score (Li et al. 2010) represents the harmonic mean of the precision and recall, providing a single measure that balances the false positives and the false negatives. The precision gauges the proportion of the accurate positive identifications among all the posi- tive predictions made by the model. X-View (cross-view) (Shahroudy et al. 2016) involves training the model with data from certain camera views and testing it with data from previ- ously unseen camera views. X-Sub (cross-subject) (Shahroudy et al. 2016; Liu et al. 2019) partitions the dataset into the training and test sets, based on subject identities. X-Set (cross- 1 3 31 Page 26 of 57 X. Top-1 and Top-5 metrics are straightforward indicators of performance, representing the percentage of instances in which the model’s highest and top five probability outputs, respectively, include the correct label. The human motion prediction extensively employs MPJPE and the mean angle error (MAE) (Lyu et al. 2022) to measure the joint coordinate errors and joint angle errors, respec- tively, to evaluate the accuracy of the prediction results. A detailed analysis of Tables 3 and 4 reveals several key trends in graph-based pose estimation. Early methods like SemGCN (Zhao et al. 2019) demonstrated the foundational viability of GCNs by modeling semantic relationships between joints, achieving competi- tive accuracy. However, recent top-performing methods such as PHGANet (Zhang et al. 2023) and Modulated-GCN (Zou and Tang 2021) signify a clear shift toward more sophis- ticated architectures. PHGANet’s success on the challenging MPI-INF-3DHP dataset, par- ticularly its state-of-the-art 86.9 PCK, highlights the benefit of its multi-hop graph attention mechanism, which captures complex, long-range dependencies that simpler models miss. Similarly, the effectiveness of Skeletal-GNN (Zeng et al. 2021) and its time-aware dynamic graph construction underscores the importance of adaptive topologies that can change based on the input pose, a crucial feature for handling diverse and difficult poses in the wild. This trend indicates that the field is moving beyond fixed graph structures toward dynamic and attention-aware models to achieve higher accuracy and robustness. The results in Table 4 reveal that SOTA performance in pose estimation is achieved through two distinct pathways: innovating on the input data representation or innovating on the graph network architecture itself. The remarkably low error of Wu et al. (2021) on Human3.6M illustrates the first pathway. Its success is not solely from its Graph Network, but primarily from its use of multi-view video data. The proposed Multi-View Matching Graph effectively fuses information from multiple camera angles, fundamentally reducing the depth ambiguity that challenges single-view methods. This highlights that enriching the input data can yield significant performance gains. In contrast, Zhang et al. (2023) exem- plifies the second pathway, achieving state-of-the-art results on the challenging MPI-INF- 3DHP benchmark through pure Graph Network architectural innovation. Its hierarchical graph attention module is specifically designed to capture complex, multi-hop dependencies between joints, demonstrating that a more sophisticated understanding of skeletal topology directly translates to higher accuracy, especially on in-the-wild data. A dominant trend is the synergistic fusion of GNNs and Transformers to harness their complementary strengths. GNNs excel at encoding local, relational inductive biases inher- ent in the human skeleton, while transformers are powerful at capturing long-range, global dependencies across all joints. A prime example of this paradigm is GCAT-Net (Qiao et al. 2025a), a novel framework that integrates a semantic GCN (SemGCN) for local topology modeling, criss-cross attention (CCA) for capturing long-range spatial dependencies, and a transformer encoder to model the temporal evolution of the pose sequence. achieved considerable success in the modeling human skeletal struc- tures and their applications. They have been adopted for the pose estimation and action recognition because of their ability to effectively encapsulate the spatial information of the human skeleton (Simonyan and Zisserman 2014). Furthermore, their intrinsic ability to con- currently model the spatio-temporal skeletal structures over video sequences (Yan et al. 2018), has led to the integration of temporal information into GCNs through the inter-frame nodal connections for the spatio-temporal correlation modeling. The simultaneous occur- rence of the spatio-temporal skeletal information has made GCNs a superior method com- pared to CNNs, RNNs, or their combination. The observations have indicated that recent research trends can pivot towards graph networks. Although the proposed methods have demonstrated the efficacy, several challenges persist and require further exploration. 5.1 Issues and challenges While graph networks have pushed the boundaries of HSM, several fundamental challenges remain. In this section, we discuss these key limitations and propose potential mitigation strategies and future research directions for each. The shallow structure of graph networks The traditional deep learning models based on CNNs typically achieve refined information features by stacking multiple convolutional layers, reducing the network parameters, and increasing the nonlinear transformations to enhance recognition performance (Li et al. 2017). However, in graph networks, experimen- tal results have indicated a decline in performance when the number of convolutional layers exceeds two (Kipf and Welling 2016). This can be because an excessively deep stack of lay- ers leads to the over-smoothing of each node within the graph, erasing distinctive features, and consequently hindering the recognition performance. To combat over-smoothing and enable deeper graph networks, researchers can draw inspiration from the success of deep CNNs. Incorporating residual or skip connections allows feature information from earlier layers to bypass intermediate layers, preserving the original node identity. Furthermore, employing attention mechanisms can help deeper layers to selectively focus on the most salient neighborhood information rather than uniformly averaging it. Advanced graph nor- malization techniques specifically designed to maintain feature variance across layers also present a promising avenue for building more powerful, deeper GCNs for HSM. The diversity of human poses and appearances The fundamental challenge in develop- ing accurate human skeletal models lies in the diversity of human skeletons (Moeslund and Granum 2001). Despite this variation, the human skeleton requires a high degree of freedom, necessitating the data-driven methods for HSM to possess sophisticated represen- tational capabilities. Moreover, image degradations such as motion blur and out-of-focus issues present in video-based data (Luo et al. 2018) impede the performance of HSM meth- ods. The adaptive capacity of graph topology is limited. During human motion, the graph topology changes with shifting actions, affecting the relationships between the nodes and 1 3 31 Page 42 of 57 X. Yang et al. the selection of key nodes. When new connections are introduced or existing associations dissolve, the graph networks exhibit the limited adaptability. Although some adaptive stud- ies have been conducted (Shi et al. 2019; Li et al. 2019), they are rule-based and cannot generate the on-the-fly dynamics. The most direct solution lies in the development of more sophisticated dynamic graph networks, as discussed in our taxonomy. These methods allow the graph’s adjacency matrix to be learned or adapted on-the-fly based on the input pose, capturing transient dependencies. A complementary approach is the use of graph attention networks, which can be viewed as a "soft" dynamic mechanism. By learning to re-weight edge importance for each specific action, attention allows the model to dynamically adjust information flow on a fixed topology. Additionally, leveraging unsupervised pre-training on massive, unlabeled video datasets could enable models to learn more robust and generaliz- able motion priors, making them inherently less sensitive to pose variations. Occlusion Current methods for HSM have exhibited the commendable performances on many public datasets. However, a well-acknowledged issue is the significant performance degradation caused by occlusions and the highly deformable nature of the human skeleton (Andriluka et al. 2014; Fang et al. 2017; Cheng et al. 2020). The self-occlusion, object occlusion, and mutual occlusion between multiple objects can prompt the modeling trunca- tion, particularly in crowded scenes (Li et al. 2019), leading to a sharp decline in model performance. Additionally, highly deformable human skeletons can create the ambiguities in small-scale human instances or certain human poses (Li et al. 2019). Consequently, there is a need for an accurate HSM method to address the challenges posed by various occlusions and individual appearances, estimate the depth of monocular images. The reason graph networks offer a fundamental improvement in occlusion resilience lies in their core operational differences from CNNs and RNNs. Methods based on CNNs oper- ate directly on pixel grids and are highly dependent on local visual evidence. When a body part is occluded by an object, its corresponding pixel information is completely replaced, and the CNN loses all direct evidence for identifying that part because it has no inher- ent understanding of the body’s global structural connectivity. On the other hand, methods based on RNNs typically process joint coordinates as a flattened sequence over time. When a joint’s coordinates are missing or inaccurate due to occlusion, the input sequence itself is corrupted. Although an RNN can use its temporal memory to make an inference, it lacks an explicit model of the body’s physical constraints and cannot understand that an occluded wrist’s position is strongly constrained by the visible elbow and shoulder. In contrast, the fundamental advantage of Graph Network is that its operational domain is a graph structure that explicitly encodes biomechanical constraints. The core mechanism of Graph Networks, message passing, allows the model to reason about a node (joint) even when its own feature information is missing. Specifically, when a wrist node is occluded, its connected and visible neighbors, such as the elbow and shoulder, can still pass "mes- sages" containing their own positional and state information to it. The Graph Network, hav- ing learned the structural priors of the skeleton during training, can then perform effective relational reasoning based on these messages to infer a plausible position for the occluded joint. This ability to leverage global topological structure to compensate for missing local information is the fundamental reason for the innate occlusion resilience of Graph Networks compared to CNNs and RNNs. 1 3 Graph network learning for human skeleton modeling: a survey Page 43 of 57 31 5.2 Comparative analysis and practitioner’s guide While the previous sections have categorized and detailed the various graph network meth- ods in HSM, a crucial question for any developer or researcher is how to choose among them. This section provides a head-to-head, critical comparison of the six categories in our taxonomy and offers a practice-oriented guide for method selection. We summarize the key characteristics of each category in Table 7. As summarized in Table 7, a clear trade-off exists between performance, cost, and appli- cability for each category. Spatio-temporal networks are the cornerstone of the field, provid- ing an efficient and powerful starting point for most tasks. Their primary limitation, a static graph structure, motivated the development of other categories. Graph attention networks and multi-scale networks can be seen as "modular" improvements upon a fixed topology, achieving a good balance between computational overhead and performance gain through more sophisticated feature aggregation. Directed graph networks and dynamic graph networks represent more fundamental, "structural" improvements, attempting to make the graph itself more intelligent. Among these, dynamic graph networks are theoretically the most expressive and are best suited for scenarios with complex human-human or human-object interaction, where the effec- tive connectivity between joints is constantly changing. This ultimate flexibility, however, comes with the highest computational cost and design complexity. Multi-stream networks offer a direct path to state-of-the-art performance, operating on the principle that more infor- mation is better. By processing and fusing different representations in parallel, such as joint positions and bone vectors, they achieve excellent results, almost always at the cost of mul- tiplied computational resources. Practitioner’s takeaway Based on this analysis, a practitioner should not seek a single "best" model, but rather make a strategic decision by weighing the core requirements and resource constraints of their specific application. For scenarios that demand a balance of performance and high efficiency, such as real- time applications like online pose tracking or large-scale video analysis, starting with a mature and lightweight spatio-temporal network is a wise and pragmatic choice. These models are generally straightforward to implement and deploy, and they serve as a powerful performance baseline for rapid project validation. To achieve targeted accuracy improvements on top of this baseline, modular enhance- ments are the next logical step. If the application requires the precise capture of subtle or key-part motions, as found in medical rehabilitation analysis or human-computer inter- action with fine-grained gestures, incorporating a graph attention mechanism is an effec- tive upgrade path. It allows the model to adaptively focus on the most informative body parts, and its attention maps can sometimes offer a degree of interpretability. Therefore, mining new node features and establishing diverse types of graphs can be crucial in future studies. The flexibility of graph networks can be fully exploited to establish more types of graphs and analyze nonstructural data. For the HSM tasks, addi- tional visual features, such as interactive features, scene graphs, and RGB characteristics, can be introduced along with the existing coordinates and appearance features at each node of the skeleton graph. Integrating the contextual information (e.g., image scenes, objects, and interactions) with the skeletal data in graph models has achieved considerable success in certain applications such as action recognition (Yan et al. 2018; Si et al. 2019; Dong et al. 2020). Combining these elements within the framework of graph networks and merging the interactions between human skeletons and scenes facilitates the enhanced graph-network- based skeletal modeling. Unsupervised learning Fully supervised methods currently dominate the field of HSM because of their superior performance, which results from the rich postural annotations in large-scale datasets. However, unlabeled images and videos makes it impractical to provide thorough annotations for these datasets. A potential avenue for future research is the explo- ration of unsupervised or weakly supervised methods for the graph-network-based skeleton modeling. For instance, Qiu et al. (2020) devised GCC, a self-supervised graph representa- tion learning framework designed to capture the universal network topological properties of multiple networks. Verma and Zhang (2019) proposed DUGNN, a deep universal graph embedding network that uses the graph kernels to learn the task-agnostic graph embeddings on different datasets. Shu et al. (2023) introduced a multi-granularity anchor contrastive representation learning approach, which learns the multi-granularity representations cover- ing the local, contextual, and global views by performing the cross-granularity and intra- granularity contrastive prediction tasks on the learnable and structurally linked skeletons. Unsupervised learning capable of automatically learning human skeletons from limitless amounts of data has emerged as an important direction to consider. Multimodality Occlusion and self-occlusion problems significantly limit the performance of the model in complex scenarios. Especially in multi-person scenarios or large changes in perspective, the model may not be able to accurately locate key points or predict skeletal movement. Future research can develop a multimodal learning framework to enhance the robustness of the model. In particular, the topological modeling ability of the graph network is used to effectively integrate skeletal information from different modes, so as to maintain high accuracy in the occlusion situation. At the same time, exploring long-range depen- dency modeling based on time-sequence relationships also helps to solve the problem of dynamic occlusion. Significant strides have been made through innovative strategies, such as attention mechanisms, multi-stream fusion, and dynamic configurations. Many models (Shi et al. 2020; Liu et al. 2020c; Cheng et al. 2020b) use fusion methods to integrate several input sequences into multi-stream architectures, combining the softmax scores of streams to achieve an aggregated score for action label prediction. Precise video-content comprehension can be substantially enhanced by leveraging the multimodality. Shi et al. (2020) demonstrate that each modality (skeleton, audio, text) brings distinct advantages, suggesting that more effective fusion strategies can elevate performance levels. Fan et al. (2020) suggested the effective inclusion of video subtitles as a source of contextual informa- 1 3 31 Page 46 of 57 X. Yang et al. tion alongside RGB video streams. However, the challenges of multimodal fusion are non- trivial, primarily stemming from three key areas: feature alignment, modality imbalance, and the selection of fusion strategy. Feature alignment addresses the difficulty of mapping heterogeneous data–such as the graph-structured skeleton data and grid-like RGB data– into a common, meaningful representation space. Modality imbalance occurs when one modality dominates the learning process, potentially overshadowing the contributions from other, sparser modalities like skeleton data. Regarding fusion strategies, they are typically categorized as early fusion (combining raw data), late fusion (combining decision scores), and hybrid fusion (combining features at intermediate layers), with each presenting its own trade-offs between information richness and architectural complexity. To elicit more distinc- tive and rich features, current multi-stream fusion frameworks tend towards complexity and high parameterization. Cai et al. (2021) proposed the application of joint flow patch (JFP) sequences to encapsulate subtle local motion details, while AdaMML (Panda et al. 2021) dynamically adapts the mode selection for each video segment. HSM plays a pivotal role in advancing fields such as artificial intelligence in AIGC and human-computer interac- tion, which enables deeper insights into human behavior in real-world environments. This burgeoning field empowers AIGC to synthesize highly realistic human motion, facilitat- ing the applications ranging from immersive entertainment with expressive virtual charac- ters to the ergonomic analysis for productivity enhancements. Integrating human posture information into large-scale language models (LLMs) enhances the semantic understand- ing, enabling them to recognize actions, intentions, and emotions. This advancement paves the way for more intuitive and impactful human-computer interaction. Xiang et al. (2023) introduced GAP for skeleton-based action recognition, which utilize a pretrained LLM to automatically generate the textual descriptions of action body part movements. RFID- ACCLDM (Wang and Mao 2024) generates the high-quality human activity data, serving as a viable substitute for real data in training human activity recognition models and achiev- ing superior performance. However, significant challenges should be addressed to real- ize these advancements. Developing the data-efficient algorithms capable of generalizing across diverse modalities and environments remains critical. As research progresses in HSM within AIGC and LLM, balancing technological advancement with ethical considerations is essential to fully harness its transformative potential. Heterogeneous graph modeling for contextual understanding Most current graph net- works model the human skeleton as a homogeneous graph, where all nodes, being the joints, and edges, being the bones, are of a single type. This paradigm excels at capturing the internal kinematics of the human body but inherently treats the body as an isolated sys- tem. Human behavior, however, is deeply embedded in its surrounding context. To break this limitation, a significant trend is the evolution toward heterogeneous graph modeling. A heterogeneous graph allows the network to contain multiple types of nodes and edges. For instance, nodes can represent not only joints but also body parts, objects in the scene, or even abstract action concepts. Edges can then represent not only physical connections but also human-object interactions, semantic relationships between joints, or part-whole hierarchies. The shift to heterogeneous graphs is significant because it enables graph networks to move beyond pure geometric analysis and begin performing true context-aware reasoning. 1 3 Graph network learning for human skeleton modeling: a survey Page 47 of 57 31 By explicitly integrating scene information into the graph structure, models can potentially handle occlusion more robustly or disambiguate actions by understanding human-object interactions. HetGCN (Gao et al. 2023) dynamically analyzes pairwise interactions and heterogeneous context aggregation between each node and its spatio-temporal neighbors to capture rich semantic representations from skeleton-based graphs. While research on explicitly constructing and applying large-scale heterogeneous graphs is still nascent, this direction represents a key future breakthrough for the HSM field: moving skeleton analysis out of a vacuum and into the rich, dynamic context of the real world. Robust HSM with principled uncertainty modeling As previously discussed, occlusion and noise introduce significant data uncertainty in HSM. Current graph network models typically learn to handle this uncertainty in an end-to-end, implicit manner, for instance by directly regressing what they determine to be the most likely joint position. This approach, however, lacks formal theoretical guidance, and the reliability of its output can be ques- tionable under high uncertainty. A more promising direction involves adopting principled uncertainty management frameworks from other mathematical fields. Three-way decision theory offers such a powerful framework. It posits that when faced with uncertain information, a decision should not be a simple binary choice of acceptance or rejection, but should include a third option of delay, thereby partitioning elements into a positive region, a negative region, and a boundary region. In the context of HSM, this means a future model could process an occluded joint not by forcing a specific coordinate out- put, but by classifying its state into one of three categories: accepted as accurately located, rejected as noise or an error, or placed in a boundary state for deferment, requiring fusion with other modalities or evidence from subsequent frames for a final decision. This deferred decision mechanism can effectively prevent the model from making high-risk, erroneous judgments when information is insufficient. Recent advances in uncertainty research, such as 3WD-FGBRS (Yang et al. 2025a) and 3WC-SGBs (Yang et al. 2025b), offer sophisti- cated mathematical tools to precisely define and manage these uncertain boundary regions. Integrating these formal uncertainty modeling techniques into future Graph Network archi- tectures is a promising interdisciplinary research direction that could lead to more robust and reliable HSM systems. However, results are often reported on different datasets with varying evaluation protocols, making direct and fair comparison challenging. A large-scale study that re-implements key models under a single, unified framework to provide a truly objective comparison–as astutely suggested during our review process–would be a significant service to the community. JSON: Name: hetero_dyn_graph_hsm Title: Dynamic heterogeneous graph neural network with three-way uncertainty modeling for robust human skeleton modeling under occlusion and multimodal conditions Short Hypothesis: Integrating a dynamic heterogeneous graph neural network with an explicit three-way decision uncertainty module and multimodal fusion causes a statistically significant reduction in 3D joint MPJPE and a statistically significant increase in skeleton-based action recognition Top-1 accuracy under occlusion compared to static homogeneous GCN baselines. Related Work: Graph-based HSM methods split into innovations on graph topology (dynamic graphs, directed graphs) and on operational modules (spatio-temporal GCNs, attention, multi-scale, multi-stream fusion). Spatio-temporal GCNs (fixed skeleton topology) established strong baselines but suffer from static adjacency, limited long-range modeling, and over-smoothing when deep. Graph attention and multi-scale networks improve per-node weighting and hierarchical receptive fields but do not fully address rapidly changing functional relations. Dynamic graph methods adapt topology but are often computationally expensive and unstable; directed graphs capture causal/hierarchical dependencies but remain mostly homogeneous (single node/edge type). Multi-stream and multimodal works improve accuracy by complementing skeletons with visual cues but face alignment and modality-imbalance issues. Prior works rarely provide principled uncertainty outputs for occluded/ambiguous joints and seldom model heterogeneous node types (joints, parts, objects) jointly; reproducibility and benchmarking across occlusion conditions and multimodal setups remain limited. Abstract: We propose a unified framework that combines dynamic heterogeneous graph neural networks with explicit three-way decision uncertainty modeling and multimodal fusion for robust human skeleton modeling. The method represents skeletons, body parts, and scene entities as distinct node types within a time-varying graph whose adjacency adapts to input-dependent functional relations; a three-way decision module classifies node estimates as accepted, rejected, or deferred (boundary) to expose calibrated uncertainty in occluded or ambiguous conditions. Multimodal streams (joint coordinates, bone vectors, and RGB-derived joint-local motion patches) are fused via a gated fusion block guided by graph-attention weights. The primary contributions are (1) a dynamic heterogeneous graph formulation for joint, part, and object reasoning across time, (2) an integrated three-way uncertainty head producing interpretable acceptance/deferment decisions, and (3) a multimodal fusion strategy conditioned on learned graph priors. Expected outcomes are improved 2D/3D pose accuracy, more reliable occlusion handling, and higher skeleton-based action recognition performance under adverse viewpoints and missing-data scenarios. Experiments: Datasets: Human3.6M (3D pose), MPI-INF-3DHP (in-the-wild 3D), MSCOCO keypoints (2D), NTU RGB+D 120 and Kinetics-skeleton (action recognition), 3DPW for outdoor 3D evaluation. Preprocessing: normalize skeletons to root-centered coordinates; compute bone vectors and extract joint-local optical-flow patches from RGB. Baselines: ST-GCN, CTR-GCN, MS-G3D, Skeletal-GNN, JOLO-GCN (or nearest reported multimodal baseline), and a Transformer-based temporal baseline. Metrics: MPJPE and PCK for 3D/2D pose; AP/AR, Top-1/Top-5 accuracy and F1 for action recognition; MAE for motion prediction at 80/160/320/1000 ms; calibration metrics (expected calibration error) and three-way acceptance rate. Training: SGD with momentum 0.9 or AdamW where baseline uses same; initial LR 1e-3 with cosine decay; batch size 64 (adjust per GPU), train for 100 epochs, repeat 3 seeds. Hardware: 4×A100 GPUs. Occlusion robustness tests: synthetic occlusion (random joint masking) at 0%, 10%, 30%, 50% joints masked and systematic occlusion of limbs; report metric degradation curves. Multimodal ablation: compare (a) skeleton-only, (b) skeleton+bone, (c) skeleton+RGB, (d) full multimodal. Graph ablation: (1) homogeneous static topology, (2) homogeneous dynamic topology, (3) heterogeneous static, (4) heterogeneous dynamic. Uncertainty ablation: (i) no uncertainty head (point estimate), (ii) probabilistic output (Gaussian), (iii) three-way decision output. Statistical analysis: paired t-tests between proposed model and top baseline for primary metrics; present per-class action recall. Runtime: report forward latency and FLOPs. Reproducibility: release code, pre-trained weights, and fixed evaluation scripts. Risk Factors and Limitations: Training instability and optimization difficulty due to jointly learning dynamic adjacency, heterogeneous node types, and multimodal fusion may cause slow convergence or mode collapse. Computational cost and memory demands of dynamic heterogeneous graphs with multimodal inputs may preclude real-time deployment on edge devices. Three-way decision thresholds require careful calibration; miscalibration can yield excessive deferment or overconfidence. Synthetic occlusion evaluations may not fully reflect real-world occlusion patterns, introducing evaluation bias. Dataset biases (demographics, action distribution, camera setups) limit generalization to unseen environments and populations. Alignment errors between RGB-derived local patches and skeleton joints can introduce noisy modalities that degrade performance. Overfitting to benchmark datasets or to multimodal synchronization patterns is possible, reducing transferability. The approach assumes sufficient multimodal data availability; performance will degrade in pure-skeleton or single-view-limited settings.
